Get started with surveyBurden

Source: vignettes/surveyBurden.Rmd
surveyBurden.Rmd

surveyBurden measures how much work a survey asks of the people who answer it. It reads a programmed Qualtrics survey, scores every question in GfS+ points, follows the survey’s flow and display logic to find the paths through it, and reports how burden varies across those paths. All of this works from the survey alone, before fieldwork.

The survey literature calls this objective burden. It is the work a survey asks of respondents, measured from the questions themselves (how many there are and how much effort each takes to answer). Perceived burden, how burdensome respondents feel the survey to be, is measured separately, for example by asking respondents directly (Yan and Williams 2022).

GfS stands for Gesellschaft für Sozialforschung (Society for Social Research), the Zürich organisation whose point system for budgeting face-to-face interviews Axhausen and colleagues adapted to self-administered surveys (Schmid and Axhausen 2019). surveyBurden uses the current version of their table (Heimgartner and Axhausen 2024) and adds documented rules for further question types, hence the “+”.

This article gets you to a first report. The function you need depends on what you have.

What you have Start with What you get Guide
A Qualtrics survey (.qsf or API) burden_report(qsf) the full report, with burden across the survey’s paths vignette("reading-the-report")
A response export respondent_burden(qsf, responses) the burden each respondent was shown vignette("respondent-burden")
A response export with completion times validate_times(qsf, observed) a check of respondent burden against time taken, and a points-per-minute rate for your survey vignette("calibration")
A draft you want to shorten burden_report() before and after an edit where the burden is, why, and how much an edit removes vignette("survey-revision")
A survey from another platform score_burden(validate_catalogue(catalogue)) a score for each question and a survey total vignette("extensions")

The other articles go deeper.

  • vignette("reading-the-report") explains each part of the printed report.
  • vignette("survey-revision") finds the heaviest parts of a draft and compares burden before and after an edit.
  • vignette("gfs-scoring") shows how a Qualtrics question becomes points, and which rules the automatic scorer applies.
  • vignette("paths-and-display-logic") covers flow, skip logic and the difference between a path and a respondent’s path.
  • vignette("calibration") covers the words_per_line and points-per-minute assumptions, checking scores against completion times, and the limitations.
  • vignette("respondent-burden") measures respondent burden from response data and prepares data for modelling break-off.
  • vignette("extensions") shows what works for surveys from other platforms, and what full support for another platform would take.

Install 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pmpk20/surveyBurden")

One call 

library(surveyBurden)
#> 
#>                   .-- Q2 -- Q3 --.
#>   survey -- Q1 --+               +-- Burden 0.3.1
#>                   '-- Q4 --------'
#> 
#> Measuring the Response Burden of Web Surveys
#> Docs: https://pmpk20.github.io/surveyBurden/
#> 
#> Please cite: King P (2026). surveyBurden: Measuring the Response Burden
#> of Web Surveys. R package version 0.3.1,
#> https://github.com/pmpk20/surveyBurden.
#> Use citation("surveyBurden") for BibTeX.
demo <- system.file("extdata", "demo_travel_survey.qsf", package = "surveyBurden")

burden_report() runs the whole pipeline. Every code chunk in these articles runs against the small fictional “Neighbourhood Travel Survey” that ships with the package, so the numbers shown are the numbers the current package produces. To use your own survey, replace demo with a path to a .qsf file, a bare SV_... survey ID, or a Qualtrics survey-builder URL. ?fetch_qsf explains fetching through the Qualtrics API.

report <- burden_report(demo, quiet = TRUE)
report

The printout opens with a headline. It gives the median burden of the complete paths in points and minutes, its ratio to the 399-point median of the GfS benchmark, and the range across complete paths. The sections below it are these.

  • Survey counts the questions, blocks, branch points, loop blocks and early exits.
  • Paths counts the distinct paths the flow allows, and how many run to the end of the survey or end early at a screen-out.
  • Burden gives the spread of path burden in points, minutes and an index. The index divides points by 1,500, the level above which Heimgartner and Axhausen (2024) found surveys to be rare, so an index of 1 marks a rare burden. The published benchmark is printed underneath.
  • Burden by block, Highest-burden questions, Readability diagnostics, Calculation certainty and QC warnings follow.

vignette("reading-the-report") walks through each section.

Terms used in these articles

Each term below has one fixed meaning across the package and its guides. The most important distinction is between a path, which is a possibility in the survey’s design, and a respondent’s path, which is the route one person actually took.

term meaning
path one route through the survey that its flow allows. A path is the sequence of blocks shown, given which branches are taken. It is worked out from the survey design alone.
question burden the GfS+ points for one question, from its type and structure
path burden the total question burden along one path. Display logic and loops can vary within a path, so a path has a range of burdens.
structural burden profile the burden values a path’s modelled display-logic combinations produce, each with an equal model weight (each path’s weights sum to 1). The weights describe the design. Shares of respondents come from respondent burden after fieldwork.
respondent burden the GfS+ points of every item shown to one respondent, reconstructed from their responses. It includes descriptive text and questions left blank, and counts each loop iteration (respondent_burden()).
calculation certainty for a given survey, how many parts of the calculation the model enumerates in full and how many rest on documented approximations. It diagnoses the model of the survey.
readability diagnostics counts of long question stems, long matrix labels and long grids. They signal reading load and are reported separately from the GfS+ score.

The report object

report is a structured R object, so you can pull out each part.

report$burden      # min / p25 / median / p75 / max, in points, minutes and index
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   statistic points minutes  index
#>   <fct>      <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 min          103    8.58 0.0687
#> 2 p25          114    9.5  0.076 
#> 3 median       120   10    0.08  
#> 4 p75          126   10.5  0.084 
#> 5 max          143   11.9  0.0953
head(report$items[order(-report$items$gfs_points),
                  c("question_id", "std_type", "gfs_points", "score_flag")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   question_id std_type     gfs_points score_flag
#>   <chr>       <chr>             <dbl> <chr>     
#> 1 QID21       matrix               18 auto      
#> 2 QID19       matrix               14 auto      
#> 3 QID14       multi_choice         12 auto      
#> 4 QID20       matrix               12 auto      
#> 5 QID1        descriptive          11 inferred  
#> 6 QID7        matrix                8 auto

The other components are report$survey (the structural counts), report$paths (one row per path), report$blocks (burden by block), report$readability, report$certainty and report$warnings. Single settings such as the points-per-minute rate are stored as attributes, for example attr(report, "points_per_minute").

summary(report) prints the headline alone.

summary(report)
#> 
#> ── Neighbourhood Travel Survey (demo) ──────────────────────────────────────────
#> 26 questions, 12 pages, 12 blocks, 4 routes (2 complete).
#> Median burden: 120 GfS+ points (range 103-143 across 2 complete routes).
#> Expected duration in minutes: ~10 (range 9-12).
#> Relative to benchmark: 0.3x the median of 399 points.

A short worked example 

report$paths[, c("path_id", "status", "n_questions_floor",
                 "n_questions_ceiling", "burden_min", "burden_max")]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   path_id status     n_questions_floor n_questions_ceiling burden_min burden_max
#>     <int> <fct>                  <int>               <int>      <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1       1 screen_out                 2                   2         12         12
#> 2       2 screen_out                 3                   3         14         14
#> 3       3 complete                  20                  26        103        143
#> 4       4 complete                  20                  23        103        139

The two screen-out paths end early after the area check. The two complete paths differ mainly in one block that a branch shows to some respondents. Within each path, the spread from minimum to maximum comes from the survey’s optional questions and loop iterations.

References

  • Heimgartner, D. and Axhausen, K. W. (2024). Predicting response rates once again. Findings. https://doi.org/10.32866/001c.125481
  • Schmid, B. and Axhausen, K. W. (2019). Predicting response rates of all and recruited respondents: a first attempt. Findings. https://doi.org/10.32866/7827
  • Yan, T. and Williams, D. (2022). Response burden: review and conceptual framework. Journal of Official Statistics 38(4), 939–961. https://doi.org/10.2478/jos-2022-0041
